title: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan
wiki_lead:
Ustad Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan (13 October 1948 – 16 August 1997), also known as NFAK, was a Pakistani singer, Hindustani classical vocalist, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, composer, and music director. While  primarily being associated with qawwali, a form of Sufi devotional music from Pakistan and India, he belonged to the historic Qawwal Bachchon ka Gharana (Delhi Gharana) and was trained in pure classical khayal architecture under his father Ustad Fateh Ali Khan and later uncle Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan and Ustad Salamat Ali Khan. Though widely celebrated for his qawwali performances, his standing as a master of Shastriya Sangeet (classical music) was validated by the classical community when he received the Hafiz Ali Khan Award in 1997. He ranks as one of the most influential South Asian singers of all time. Widely recognised as the "Shahanshah-e-Qawwali" (lit. 'the King of Kings of Qawwali'), he has been recognised as one of the 50 Great Voices by NPR and 200 Greatest Singers of All Time by Rolling Stone. The New York Times named Khan the greatest qawwali singer of his generation. while Credited with introducing Qawwali music to international audiences, he was known for his vocal abilities and could perform at a high level of intensity for several hours.
Born in West Punjab, Khan had his first public performance at the age of 15 at his father's chelum. He became the head of the family qawwali party in 1971 and added his unique style of sargam, khayal, and rhythm to his family's legacy. He was signed by Oriental Star Agencies, based in Birmingham, England, in the early 1980s. Khan went on to release movie scores and albums in Europe, India, Japan, Pakistan, and the United States. He engaged in collaborations and experiments with Western artists, becoming a well-known world music artist. He toured extensively, performing in over 40 countries. In addition to popularising qawwali music, he also had a profound impact on contemporary South Asian popular music, including Pakistani pop, Indian pop, and Bollywood music. He was also a master of Hindustani classical music.

Biography


Early life

Khan was born into a Punjabi Muslim family in Lyallpur in 1948. Khan's family belonged to Jalandhar. His ancestors learned music and singing there and adopted it as a profession. He was the fifth child and first son of Fateh Ali Khan, a musicologist, vocalist, instrumentalist, and qawwal. Nusrat, who had four older sisters and a younger brother, Farrukh Fateh Ali Khan, grew up in central Faisalabad. The tradition of qawwali in the family has been passed down through successive generations for almost 600 years. This qawwali tradition has also been preserved by other family members, such as his cousins Badar Miandad and Sher Miandad Khan. Initially, his father did not want Khan to follow the family's vocation. He had his heart set on Nusrat choosing a career path that commanded greater respect in society and wanted him to become a doctor or engineer because he felt qawwali artists had low social status. However, Khan showed such an aptitude for and interest in qawwali that his father finally relented.


Early career
In his youth, Nusrat joined his father's qawwali party as a tabla player whilst continuing to learn the intricacies of singing. When Ustad Munawar Ali Khan, son of legendary classical vocalist Ustad Bade Ghulam Ali Khan, visited Pakistan from India to perform, Nusrat accompanied him on tabla. Munawar Ali Khan's enthusiastic praise for Nusrat's playing helped convince his father to stop pressuring him to become a doctor.
Following the death of his father, Fateh Ali Khan, in 1964, Nusrat became the lead singer of the qawwali party in 1965 alongside his uncle, Mubarak Ali Khan. The party also included Mujahid Mubarak Ali Khan, the son of Mubarak and the cousin of Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan. grok_lead: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan (13 October 1948 â 16 August 1997) was a Pakistani singer, songwriter, and musician widely regarded as one of the greatest exponents of qawwali, a devotional form of Sufi music originating from the Indian subcontinent. Born in Faisalabad (then Lyallpur), Punjab, into a family of qawwals with over 600 years of musical tradition, he became the 20th generation performer following the death of his father, Ustad Fateh Ali Khan, in 1964. Khan's powerful vocal range, improvisational style, and ability to evoke spiritual ecstasy defined his performances, which often lasted hours and blended poetry from Sufi saints like Amir Khusrau with rhythmic harmonium and tabla accompaniment. Over his career, he recorded more than 125 albums, earning a Guinness World Record for the most recordings by a qawwali artist, and received Pakistan's Pride of Performance award in 1987 for his contributions to national culture. Khan began his professional career in the late 1960s as the leader of his family's Qawwali Party, a troupe of nine musicians including relatives like his brother Farrukh Fateh Ali Khan on harmonium. He modernized qawwali by shortening traditional multi-hour sessions to 15-25 minutes for broader appeal, while preserving its ecstatic, trance-like essence rooted in Islamic mysticism and Punjabi folk influences. Early recordings focused on devotional songs praising the Prophet Muhammad and Sufi figures, gaining popularity in Pakistan and India through live performances at shrines and festivals. His breakthrough to international audiences came in 1985 at the WOMAD festival in the UK, where his set of songs like "Allah Ho" and "Haq Ali Ali" captivated secular crowds, marking a pivotal moment in global world music. In the 1990s, Khan expanded into fusion genres, collaborating with Western producers to bridge Eastern and Western sounds. Notable works include the album Mustt Mustt (1990) with Canadian producer Michael Brook, which blended qawwali with ambient electronica, and Night Song (1996), a Grammy-nominated project featuring guests like Peter Gabriel and Eddie Vedder. His vocals also appeared in Hollywood films, including Martin Scorsese's The Last Temptation of Christ (1988), Oliver Stone's Natural Born Killers (1994), and Tim Robbins' Dead Man Walking (1995), introducing qawwali to global cinema audiences. Khan's innovative approach earned praise from artists like Jeff Buckley, who called him "my Elvis," and solidified his role as a cultural ambassador. Khan died of cardiac arrest in London at age 48, leaving a profound legacy as the "Shahenshah-e-Qawwali" (Emperor of Qawwali), whose music continues to inspire genres from electronica to hip-hop and influences contemporary performers like his nephew Rahat Fateh Ali Khan. His recordings, including timeless tracks like " Afreen Afreen " and "Dam Mast Qalandar," remain staples in South Asian music, with more than 125 albums ensuring his voice endures as a symbol of spiritual and artistic transcendence.
